editions.label: 28 Aug
editions.title: Orion buys 72% of Corinthia Lisbon for €102M as hotels lead a €1.4bn investment year
editions.summary: Orion Capital Managers has bought 72% of the Corinthia Lisbon — the capital's largest five-star hotel — for about €102 million, via a Luxembourg JV that leaves brand-owner IHI with 28% and the operating keys. It's Orion's third Portuguese bet, after Oriente Green Campus and developer Vizta. The timing is no accident: hospitality now tops commercial investment, drawing €508M in H1 2026 (+54%) — 36% of a €1.4bn half-year, per Savills. On the other side of the cycle, Novo Banco is listing €400M of Luís Filipe Vieira's property to claw back debt. And the housing engine keeps running hot: Q2 sales rose 7% and licensing hit its highest since 2011. Net: foreign institutional money is crowding into Portuguese hotels and bank-driven distress at the same moment supply finally starts to move.

editions.label: 27 Aug
editions.title: Foreign capital drives 65% of Portugal's €1.42bn H1 real-estate haul; Clarion buys in
editions.summary: Foreign money is running Portugal's market — and it's still buying. Overseas capital drove 65% of Portugal's €1.42bn commercial real-estate spend in H1 (JLL), with hotels (34%) and retail (32%) taking two-thirds and offices lagging at 6%. This week the thesis walked on stage: US manager Clarion Partners bought a Malveira supermarket let long-term to Portugal's biggest grocer. In housing, developers keep pressing — Mesmo Valor is putting €75M into a 24-storey Boavista tower — even as INE data shows price growth decelerating for the first time in nearly two years. Regulators are moving on short-term lets and capital-gains relief. Net: capital is abundant and cross-border, but the buy-side is turning selective — income-secure assets and prime resi still clear.

editions.label: 26 Aug
editions.title: Orion buys 72% of Lisbon's Corinthia for €102M as hotel capital keeps pouring in
editions.summary: Hotel capital is pouring into Portugal — and Lisbon's biggest just changed hands. Orion Capital paid €102M for 72% of the Corinthia Lisbon, valuing the capital's largest five-star hotel at roughly €142M. It's the clearest sign yet that hospitality is Portugal's hottest real-estate trade in 2026, with hotels and retail already leading a commercial market up 11% to €1.4bn in H1. The pipeline is thick: Amorim Luxury opens its first hotel on Avenida da Liberdade in October, and the Tivoli owners are scouting two more in the north. Logistics is just as tight — VGP's new Sintra park pre-let 100% before completion. The flip side is the housing squeeze: only 7% of students can find beds, shared-room demand is up 27% as supply falls, and lawmakers are moving on both short-term lets and condominium rules. Net: money is chasing yield in hotels and sheds while the state tightens its grip on homes.

editions.label: 25 Aug
editions.title: Portugal resets the short-let clock: big cities get to Dec 31 to rewrite AL rules
editions.summary: Portugal's short-let rulebook just bought itself another year. A new decree-law — 151/2026 — hands every município with 1,000-plus registered short-lets until 31 December 2026 to finalise, or suspend, local Alojamento Local rules. Councils can renew an existing registration freeze once more, but every suspension must end by year's close. It lands as the rental squeeze sharpens: room supply fell 11% in Q2 while demand jumped 27%, pushing Lisbon rooms to €550. Capital, meanwhile, keeps arriving — €1.42bn flowed into commercial property in H1, roughly three-quarters of it foreign, with hospitality still leading. Two Lisbon palaces underline the appetite: one becoming 46 apartments in Arroios, another a Barrière luxury hotel in Príncipe Real. Net: the rules are still being drawn — but the money isn't waiting for them.

editions.label: 24 Aug
editions.title: SOLYD buys Alta de Lisboa lot for 300 homes; CBRE & JLL market Maia logistics
editions.summary: Land is moving. SOLYD Property Developers has bought a ~10,000 m² lot in Alta de Lisboa, enough for roughly 300 homes across four blocks plus retail — a rare speculative land bet in a supply-starved city. Up north, CBRE and JLL are marketing the Folgosa I&II logistics assets near Porto — 11,000 m² of scarce quality warehousing put up by Proxity. Policy is bending toward supply too: APPII is backing a rental-law overhaul it says could finally seed a build-to-rent market, while municipalities gain new expropriation powers and Porto tightens the screws on short-lets. And the money keeps flowing — Portuguese construction output rose 1.2% in June even as the eurozone shrank. Net: the pipeline is filling from both ends — land deals at the top, reform at the base.

editions.label: 22 Aug
editions.title: Hotel money surges 54% as €1.42bn pours into Portuguese commercial property
editions.summary: Capital is rotating hard into Portuguese bricks — hotels above all. Commercial real-estate investment hit €1.42bn in H1 2026, up 11% year-on-year, per JLL. Hotels led the charge: €508m flowed into Portuguese hotels in H1, a 54% jump, with Corinthia Lisbon, Penha Longa and InterContinental Porto alone worth €350m. Real estate was the single most active M&A sector — 44 deals — even as overall dealmaking cooled 28% to €4.5bn. Nearly all the hotel money, 95.6%, came from abroad. Meanwhile the squeeze on households deepened: renting now swallows 82% of income nationally, and 101% in Faro. Net: foreign capital is still betting heavily on Portuguese yield — even as ordinary buyers and renters get priced out.

editions.label: 21 Aug
editions.title: Portugal H1 hotel deals hit €508M, up 54%; commercial investment reaches €1.42bn
editions.summary: Portugal pulled in €1.42bn of commercial real-estate investment in H1, up 11% on last year, JLL says. Hotels led the charge — €508m in six months, a 54% jump, with Corinthia Lisbon, Penha Longa and InterContinental Porto alone worth €350m. Retail is heating up too: Clarion Partners just bought a Malveira supermarket, and Sonae Sierra and Norway's Norges are hunting Portuguese malls after a €1.5bn Spanish spree. Developers are moving on land and heritage — SOLYD landed a lot for ~300 homes in Alta de Lisboa. And the clock is ticking on rules: the new accessible-rental regimes go live 1 September. Net: money is abundant and foreign (65% of deals); the scarce thing is product.

editions.label: 20 Aug
editions.title: SOLYD buys Alta de Lisboa plot for ~300 homes — 10,000 m² of buildable in Lumiar
editions.summary: A rare buildable plot changed hands in Lisbon as SOLYD acquired a ~10,000 m² lot in Alta de Lisboa (Alto do Lumiar / PUAL) cleared for roughly 300 homes across four autonomous blocks plus retail — permit-ready land at scale is scarce in the capital. The structural evidence sits upstream: Portugal's Lei dos Solos has produced just 27 rustic-to-urban reclassification requests across 23 municipalities in 18 months, so new buildable supply is barely moving. On rules, Lei 48/2026 (published 17 Aug) settles the ARU/ORU fight — the 6% rehabilitation VAT now applies on ARU location alone, retroactive to 2009, a clean build-cost win for value-add. The state is pushing supply the other way, with 28,000 PRR public homes due by end-August (40,000 targeted by December). Foreign capital keeps arriving for land it can build on, led by a €13bn-plus AI data-centre pipeline (Sines, Vila Franca de Xira, Carnaxide). And construction runs hot against a cooling Europe — output +1.2% in June vs the eurozone's −0.7%, with construction the only sector adding companies (+5.7%). Net: shovel-ready land is repricing upward as approvals lag demand.

editions.label: 19 Aug
editions.title: The affordability squeeze becomes the market's defining story as prices set a ninth straight record
editions.summary: Fresh idealista data put national rents at 82% of net household income and purchase costs at 76% — more than double the 33% comfort threshold — even as asking prices hit a ninth consecutive record at €3,210/m² (+8% YoY). Into that tension, Banco de Portugal's tighter mortgage rule took effect, cutting the debt-service cap from 50% to 45% and threatening to shave 10–15% off new-loan approvals. The state is answering on supply with 28,000 PRR public homes due by month-end, but that capital sits in the affordable segment, leaving mid-market, prime and rental to private players. The widening wedge — owner-occupiers priced out, institutional and rental capital stepping in — keeps strengthening the build-to-rent and value-add case.
